title_en: Jiangsu Foreign Enterprise Co., Ltd. v. Shanghai Fengtai Insurance Co., Ltd. — dispute over marine cargo transportation insurance contract
ruling_gist_en: If the insured fails to disclose to the insurer, between the time of applying for insurance and the formation of the insurance contract, all material circumstances that the insured knows or ought to know in the ordinary course of business and that are sufficient to influence the insurer's decision on whether to underwrite and how to determine the premium, the insured violates the principle of utmost good faith, and the insurer may declare the insurance contract void on that ground.
keywords_en: Civil; Dispute over marine cargo insurance contract; First instance; Shanghai Maritime Court; Jiangsu Province; Shanghai Municipality; Legal person; UK Marine Insurance Act 1906; Whether failure to disclose known loss at the time of insurance application violates the principle of utmost good faith; Whether the insurance contract is void for non-disclosure of material circumstances; Whether insurance liability commences from the formation of the insurance contract; Dismissal of claims; Marine cargo transportation; Total loss of cargo; Known cargo loss not disclosed at the time of insurance application; Backdated insurance policy; Principle of utmost good faith; Contract dispute; Sales contract; Insurance contract
full_text_en:
Jiangsu Foreign Enterprise Group v. Shanghai Fengtai Insurance (Asia) Co., Ltd., Shanghai Branch — Dispute over Marine Cargo Insurance Contract

Ruling Summary

Where an insured party, between the time of applying for insurance and the conclusion of the insurance contract, fails to disclose to the insurer all material circumstances which are known to the insured, or ought to be known in the ordinary course of business, and which are sufficient to influence the insurer's decision whether to accept the risk and at what premium, the insured has violated the principle of utmost good faith, and the insurer may avoid the insurance contract.

Plaintiff: Jiangsu Overseas Enterprise Group Co., Ltd., domiciled at: Beijing East Road, Nanjing, Jiangsu Province.

Legal Representative: Yang Dawei, Chairman of the Board of the said company.

Defendant: Fengtai Insurance (Asia) Co., Ltd., Shanghai Branch, domiciled at: Lujiazui Road, Shanghai.

Responsible Person: Yuan Jiexin, General Manager of the said branch.

The plaintiff, Jiangsu Overseas Enterprise Group Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as "Jiangsu Foreign Enterprise"), filed a lawsuit with the Shanghai Maritime Court against the defendant, Fengtai Insurance (Asia) Co., Ltd., Shanghai Branch (hereinafter referred to as "Shanghai Fengtai Insurance"), concerning a dispute over a marine cargo insurance contract.

Plaintiff’s Allegations: The plaintiff purchased 5,688.407 cubic meters of timber from French Company S, valued at USD 1,134,956.63. After the goods were shipped from abroad on September 12, 1999, the plaintiff completed three cargo insurance proposal forms to apply for insurance with the defendant, with a total insured amount of USD 1,248,452.29. On October 21 of the same year, Company S notified the plaintiff by fax that the vessel carrying the insured goods had sunk due to a storm, resulting in a total loss of the cargo. At the time of applying for insurance, no one had reported this maritime casualty to the plaintiff; therefore, this casualty fell within the scope of the defendant's coverage. On November 8 of the same year, the plaintiff reported the loss to the defendant and requested indemnity. The defendant refused the plaintiff's claim, on the grounds that its insurance liability had not yet commenced at the time of the insured event, and that the insurance contract between the parties was void. The plaintiff requests the court to order the defendant to pay insurance compensation of USD 1,248,452.29, plus interest on this amount, and to bear the litigation costs.

The plaintiff submitted the following evidence:
1. The cargo sales contract, cargo invoice, trade letter of credit, original bills of lading, etc., to prove the name, quantity, and price of the subject matter insured, as well as the name of the carrying vessel and the sailing date.
2. A letter from China Merchants Bank, Nanjing Branch, to Jiangsu Foreign Enterprise, and bank payment vouchers, to prove that Jiangsu Foreign Enterprise had paid the purchase price for the goods in question.
3. Three copies each of the proposal forms and the insurance policies issued by Shanghai Fengtai Insurance, to prove that Shanghai Fengtai Insurance agreed to insure the goods in question.
4. Written testimony from Zhu Hua, an employee of Jiangsu Foreign Enterprise, to prove that Jiangsu Foreign Enterprise received the insurance policies for the goods in question on October 14, 1999.
5. A counterfoil of a check signed by Yu Yongbin, a business clerk of Shanghai Fengtai Insurance, to prove that Shanghai Fengtai Insurance received the premium paid by Jiangsu Foreign Enterprise before October 18, 1999, and that the insurance contract between the parties had been concluded.
6. A fax dated October 21, 1999, from the foreign seller to Jiangsu Foreign Enterprise notifying it of the cargo loss, to prove that Jiangsu Foreign Enterprise learned of the cargo loss only after applying for insurance.
7. A claim letter dated November 8, 1999, from Jiangsu Foreign Enterprise to Shanghai Fengtai Insurance, and three letters from Shanghai Fengtai Insurance refusing the claim, to prove the exchange between the parties after the cargo loss occurred.
8. A letter of authorization and a receipt from Shanghai Fengtai Insurance entrusting McLarens International Group to inspect the cargo loss in question, to prove that McLarens International Group had received from Jiangsu Foreign Enterprise the insurance policies, bills of lading, invoices, and packing lists relating to the goods in question, and had conducted an inspection of the goods.

Defendant’s Defense: On October 14, 1999, the plaintiff applied for insurance with the defendant, stating that the insured goods had been loaded on board the vessel on September 12 of that year, and requested that the date on the insurance policy be backdated to September 12. The defendant considered that the plaintiff's request was a common practice in international trade to facilitate settlement, and should be allowed, but the plaintiff must warrant that, on or before October 14, the date of the insurance application, there was no known or reported loss concerning the insured goods. On October 20, the defendant delivered to the plaintiff the insurance policies with dates backdated to September 12. The facts of this case are that the vessel carrying the insured goods had been abandoned as early as October 11 due to a perils of the sea, that this maritime casualty was reported by the French media and on the Lloyd's List website on October 12, and that the seller of the goods and the shipowner had also notified the plaintiff of this news on October 14. Therefore, the plaintiff applied for insurance knowing that the goods were already damaged. Furthermore, the original bills of lading submitted by the plaintiff contained a notation indicating that part of the goods in question was loaded on deck. This was an important fact that would affect the defendant's decision whether to insure these goods. The plaintiff never disclosed this important fact to the defendant, thereby affecting the defendant's ability, as an insurer, to make a correct determination as to whether it could insure these goods. The defendant should not be liable for losses that occurred before the insurance contract was concluded. The plaintiff violated the principle of utmost good faith by concealing important facts that could affect the conclusion of the insurance contract. The defendant has the right to declare the insurance contract void. The plaintiff's claims should be dismissed.

The defendant submitted the following evidence:
1. A fax copy of the proposal form and the registration form for issuing the insurance policy, to prove that the actual time of Jiangsu Foreign Enterprise's insurance application was October 14, 1999.
2. The insurance policy, Shanghai Fengtai Insurance's internal policy issuance receipt record, premium receipt, bank credit memo, blank standard form insurance policies, premium notice, and several standard form policies actually used by Shanghai Fengtai Insurance when entering into insurance contracts with third parties, to prove that in actual business practice, the printing date of Shanghai Fengtai Insurance's insurance policies should be the same as the printing date of the premium notice, and thus to prove that the insurance policy in this case was issued on October 18, 1999, and that Jiangsu Foreign Enterprise could only have obtained the policy after that date.
3. Written testimony from Yan Zhen, Ding Jiayu, and Ding Yong, employees of Shanghai Fengtai Insurance, to prove the process of applying for insurance for the goods in question and that Jiangsu Foreign Enterprise refused to provide a written warranty that it was unaware of any loss to the subject matter insured at the time of applying for insurance.
4. A preliminary report on the inspection of the cargo loss by McLarens International Group and a written testimony from Michael H. Siu-keung, an employee of McLarens International Group, to prove the circumstances of the inspection of the cargo loss.
5. A sworn statement (notarized and authenticated) from Jean-Louis Archambeau, the insurance adjuster for the goods in question, and its attachments, and a report on the casualty involving the vessel in question downloaded from the Lloyd's List website and signed by Hong Kong witness Wu Xiaomei, to prove that Jiangsu Foreign Enterprise knew as early as before October 14, 1999, that the carrying vessel in question had been abandoned due to a perils of the sea.
6. A letter dated January 27, 2000, from Jiangsu Foreign Enterprise to Shanghai Fengtai Insurance, to prove that Jiangsu Foreign Enterprise had not yet negotiated the letter of credit in question and therefore had no insurable interest in the goods in question.
7. An English copy and Chinese translation of the Marine Insurance Act 1906 of the United Kingdom, to prove the relevant content of the law applicable to this case.

The court presided over the examination of the evidence and made the following determinations regarding the evidence submitted by both parties:

Among the evidence submitted by the plaintiff, Evidence 4 (written testimony of the plaintiff's internal employee) is not confirmed due to the lack of other corroborating evidence; except for this, the other evidence is confirmed as the defendant raised no objections to their form or content. Among the evidence submitted by the defendant, Evidence 1, Evidence 2, the insurance adjuster's statement in Evidence 5, Evidence 6, and Evidence 7 are confirmed as the plaintiff raised no objections to their form or content; Evidence 3 (written testimony of the defendant's internal employees) is not confirmed due to the lack of other corroborating evidence; the qualifications for conducting the inspection referred to in Evidence 4 are not proven by any evidence, so the validity of Evidence 4 is not confirmed; the attachments to the insurance adjuster's statement and the report downloaded from the Lloyd's List website in Evidence 5 were obtained from abroad and have not been notarized or authenticated, so their validity is not confirmed.

After examination and verification of the evidence, the Shanghai Maritime Court finds the following facts:

On July 16, 1999, the plaintiff, Jiangsu Foreign Enterprise, as buyer, entered into a trade agreement with French Company S for the import of 10,000 cubic meters of timber. The terms were: the timber was to be shipped from the port of Gabon, France, and transported to Zhangjiagang Port, China; the price was USD 197 per cubic meter, payment to be made by irrevocable letter of credit 90 days after the bill of lading was issued; the buyer was responsible for marine insurance based on the seller's advice. On July 23, China Merchants Bank, Nanjing Branch, issued an irrevocable letter of credit in favor of Company S for a total amount of USD 1,970,000, upon the application of Jiangsu Foreign Enterprise. On September 12, the carrier, French company SETRAMAR, issued two original clean bills of lading for 5,688.407 cubic meters of timber carried on the vessel "SANAGA".

On October 14, 1999, the plaintiff, Jiangsu Foreign Enterprise, sent three proposal forms by fax to the defendant, Shanghai Fengtai Insurance, requesting that Shanghai Fengtai Insurance issue insurance policies for the above-mentioned transported timber with the following content: the policyholder was Jiangsu Foreign Enterprise; the insured amounts were USD 4,777.08, USD 28,833.34, and USD 1,214,841.87, respectively; the name of the carrying vessel was "SANAGA"; the sailing date was September 12, 1999; the cargo quantities were 12.408 cubic meters, 69.899 cubic meters, and 5,606.10 cubic meters, respectively; the insurance conditions were all risks; and the policy issuance date was backdated to September 12, 1999. On the afternoon of October 14, Shanghai Fengtai Insurance made an internal policy issuance registration for the business applied for by Jiangsu Foreign Enterprise. The registration form recorded the applicant's name, the time of application, the insurance policy number, and other matters. On October 18, Shanghai Fengtai Insurance prepared three insurance policies with dates backdated to September 12. The policies stated the insurance conditions as Institute Cargo Clauses (C), Jettison and Washing Overboard Clause, Institute Classification Clause, Institute Radioactive Contamination Exclusion Clause, ISM Cargo Endorsement Clause, and Y2K Exclusion Clause, and also contained a warranty clause stating: "WARRANTED THERE IS NO KNOWN AND/OR REPORTED LOSS BEFORE 14/10/1999." During the trial, Shanghai Fengtai Insurance stated that it had modified the insurance conditions at the request of Jiangsu Foreign Enterprise. Jiangsu Foreign Enterprise did not confirm this. On October 18, these three insurance policies were signed for internally by the staff of Shanghai Fengtai Insurance who handled the insurance business.

On October 21, 1999, French Company S sent a fax to the plaintiff, Jiangsu Foreign Enterprise, stating that the carrying vessel was damaged and suggesting that Jiangsu Foreign Enterprise notify the insurance company; on October 22, Company S forwarded to Jiangsu Foreign Enterprise a fax from the carrier of the goods in question, indicating that the carrying vessel had sunk on October 14 in a severe storm 750 nautical miles from Durban, South Africa, resulting in a total loss of the cargo. On November 8, Jiangsu Foreign Enterprise reported the loss to the defendant, Shanghai Fengtai Insurance, and requested indemnity. On December 30 of the same year, and on February 21 and April 12, 2000, Shanghai Fengtai Insurance sent three letters to Jiangsu Foreign Enterprise, stating that, because Jiangsu Foreign Enterprise had breached the warranty clause on the face of the insurance policy and had failed to disclose the true situation in accordance with the principle of utmost good faith, it declared that it had the right to avoid and terminate the insurance contract, and refused to pay insurance compensation to Jiangsu Foreign Enterprise. On June 9, 2000, Jean-Louis Archambeau, an employee of French company MCLAREN STOPLIS FRANCE S.A., issued a statement declaring that, as one of the heads of the Marine Property Insurance Department of this professional insurance surveying agency, he had been entrusted by Shanghai Fengtai Insurance to conduct an insurance survey for the goods in question. According to his understanding of the circumstances of this case, on September 24, 1999, the shipper Company S submitted copies of two shipping orders for the goods in question to Jiangsu Foreign Enterprise; on October 12 of the same year, Company S received a fax from the carrier SETRAMAR, learning that the carrying vessel "SANAGA" was reportedly abandoned by the crew on October 11 due to massive water ingress; at 13:38 local time in France on October 14, Company S sent to Jiangsu Foreign Enterprise two copies of a fax from the carrier SETRAMAR concerning the cargo loss. Jiangsu Foreign Enterprise admitted to receiving the fax from Company S but argued that, because there was a seven-hour time difference between China and France, the time Jiangsu Foreign Enterprise received the fax should have been 20:38 on October 14, 1999, at which time Jiangsu Foreign Enterprise had already applied for insurance with Shanghai Fengtai Insurance. This, it argued, proved that Jiangsu Foreign Enterprise was unaware of the maritime casualty involving the carrying vessel at the time of applying for insurance. On December 24, 2002, Jiangsu Foreign Enterprise paid the issuing bank, China Merchants Bank, Nanjing Branch, the purchase price under the letter of credit, amounting to USD 1,134,956.63.

It is further found that: During the trial, the defendant, Shanghai Fengtai Insurance, stated that the reverse side of the insurance policies in question contained a governing law clause. Although neither party submitted the reverse side clauses of the insurance policies to the court, both parties had no objection to applying the Marine Insurance Act 1906 of the United Kingdom to resolve the dispute in this case, as agreed in the reverse side clause of the policies.

The disputed issues between the parties in this case are: (1) How to determine the time of conclusion of the insurance contract in question and the time of commencement of the insurance liability. (2) Whether the maritime casualty in question falls within the scope of the warranty clause in the insurance contract. (3) Whether Shanghai Fengtai Insurance can declare the insurance contract void.

The Shanghai Maritime Court holds: The subject matter of the insurance contract in question and the place of performance of the contract contain foreign elements; therefore, this case is a foreign-related insurance contract dispute.

Article 245 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China provides: "If, in a foreign-related civil action, the defendant does not raise an objection to the jurisdiction of a people's court and responds to the action and defends, he shall be deemed to have recognized that the people's court has jurisdiction." After the plaintiff, Jiangsu Foreign Enterprise, filed its lawsuit with the Shanghai Maritime Court, the defendant, Shanghai Fengtai Insurance, did not raise a jurisdictional objection and responded to the action and defended. This shall be deemed as acceptance of the Shanghai Maritime Court's jurisdiction. The Shanghai Maritime Court has the authority to try this case according to law. Article 145, Paragraph 1, of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China provides: "The parties to a foreign-related contract may choose the law applicable to the settlement of their contractual disputes, unless otherwise provided by law." In this case, both parties agreed to apply the Marine Insurance Act 1906 of the United Kingdom to resolve the dispute, as stipulated in the reverse side clause of the insurance policies. This agreement represents the true intention of the parties, does not violate the general principles and social public interests of Chinese law, and is permitted by the general conflict of laws rules of private international law. Therefore, the Marine Insurance Act 1906 of the United Kingdom shall be confirmed as the governing law for resolving the insurance contract dispute in this case. The English copy and Chinese translation of the Marine Insurance Act 1906 of the United Kingdom submitted by Shanghai Fengtai Insurance were not objected to by Jiangsu Foreign Enterprise, and after examination and verification by the court, their content is confirmed.

Regarding the time of conclusion of the insurance contract in question and the time of commencement of insurance liability: Article 21 of the Marine Insurance Act 1906 of the United Kingdom provides: "A contract of marine insurance is deemed to be concluded when the proposer's offer to the insurer is accepted by the insurer, whether the policy be then issued or not; and, for the purpose of showing when the offer was accepted, reference may be made to the slip or covering note or other customary memorandum of the contract." According to this provision, the act of the insurer accepting the proposal form is not only deemed as accepting the offer but also as making a promise. As long as the insurer fully accepts the insurance conditions listed by the insured in the proposal form, regardless of whether the insurer issues the policy at that time, the marine insurance contract is deemed to have been concluded. Article 64, Paragraph 1, of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China provides: "A party has the responsibility to provide evidence in support of its own allegations." In this case, both parties confirmed that on October 14, 1999, the plaintiff, Jiangsu Foreign Enterprise, sent proposal forms to the defendant, Shanghai Fengtai Insurance. This is the exact time when Jiangsu Foreign Enterprise made the offer. Shanghai Fengtai Insurance, relying on its own policy issuance receipt records, proved that the earliest time it delivered the insurance policies to Jiangsu Foreign Enterprise was October 18, 1999. Referring to the insurance policies issued by Shanghai Fengtai Insurance, it can be seen that they included additional warranty clauses and changes in the insurance conditions. These substantive additions and modifications to the insurance conditions prove that Shanghai Fengtai Insurance did not fully accept the offer made by Jiangsu Foreign Enterprise on October 14, 1999. Instead, it made a new offer in the issued insurance policies. Therefore, the insurance contract was not concluded at that time. Only after Jiangsu Foreign Enterprise accepted the insurance policies issued by Shanghai Fengtai Insurance on October 18, 1999, and did not raise any objection within a reasonable time, could its acceptance be deemed as a promise to conclude the insurance contract. Therefore, the earliest time of conclusion of the insurance contract in this case should be October 18, 1999. Jiangsu Foreign Enterprise stated in court that it received the insurance policies on the same day it applied for insurance, and that the insurance contract should have been concluded on October 14, 1999. However, the company did not provide valid evidence to support this claim. Therefore, this claim is not accepted.

The commencement of insurance liability is different from the time of conclusion of the insurance contract or the time of issuance of the insurance policy. Insurance liability does not necessarily commence once the insurance contract is concluded or once the insurance policy is issued. The time of conclusion of the insurance contract depends on when the acceptance reaches the offeror; the time of commencement of insurance liability depends on the agreement of the parties in the insurance contract, including the agreement in the insurance policy or a special agreement between the parties. According to the agreement of the parties in the insurance contract, the time of commencement of insurance liability may be earlier than, equal to, or later than the time of conclusion of the insurance contract. The insurance policy is merely a tool reflecting the negotiation process of the insurance contract or the specific content of the insurance contract as concluded through negotiation. Therefore, whether and when it is issued has no direct and necessary connection with the conclusion of the insurance contract or the commencement of insurance liability. The insurance contract in this case was concluded on October 18, 1999. Both parties admit that the issuance date of September 12, 1999, on the insurance policies was backdated. Whether this backdated date can be used as the time of commencement of insurance liability is not expressly stipulated in the insurance contract and must be determined through a specific analysis of the insurance contract. Jiangsu Foreign Enterprise's claim that the backdated date on the insurance policy should be used as the time of commencement of insurance liability lacks legal basis and is not accepted.

Regarding whether the marine casualty involved in this case falls within the scope of the warranty clause in the insurance contract. The insurance contract in this case contains a warranty clause: "Warranted no known or reported loss prior to October 14, 1999." The significance of this clause is to demarcate the time boundary for risk allocation between the insured and the insurer as 24:00 on October 14, 1999. Although the existing evidence cannot prove that the Plaintiff, Jiangsu Overseas Enterprise Company, knew of the loss of the insured goods prior to taking out the insurance, it can prove that the Company knew of the loss of the insured goods before 24:00 on October 14, 1999, and that the loss situation had been reported before 24:00 on October 14, 1999. Therefore, as long as the warranty clause is effective, the marine casualty in this case still falls within the scope of liability to be borne by the insured under this clause.

Jiangsu Overseas Enterprise Company's defense that it was unaware of the loss at the time of insurance, and therefore should not bear liability for the marine casualty, is untenable.

Regarding whether Shanghai Fengtai Insurance Company can declare the insurance contract void. Article 17 of the UK Marine Insurance Act 1906 provides: "A contract of marine insurance is a contract based upon the utmost good faith, and, if the utmost good faith be not observed by either party, the contract may be avoided by the other party." Articles 18(1) and (2) provide: "...the assured must disclose to the insurer, before the contract is concluded, every material circumstance which is known to the assured, and the assured is deemed to know every circumstance which, in the ordinary course of business, ought to be known by him. If the assured fails to make such disclosure, the insurer may avoid the contract. Every circumstance is material which would influence the judgment of a prudent insurer in fixing the premium, or determining whether he will take the risk." Article 20 provides: "...Every material representation made by the assured or his agent to the insurer during the negotiations for the contract, and before the contract is concluded, must be true. If it be untrue the insurer may avoid the contract. ... A representation is material which would influence the judgment of a prudent insurer in fixing the premium, or determining whether he will take the risk. ... A representation may be either a representation as to a matter of fact, or as to a matter of expectation or belief. ... A representation may be withdrawn or corrected before the contract is concluded. ..." According to the above provisions, the formation of an insurance contract shall adhere to the principle of utmost good faith. Throughout the entire process of making an offer, accepting a counter-offer, and giving acceptance, the insured shall, based on the principle of utmost good faith, truthfully inform the insurer of any material circumstances which are known to the insured or which ought to be known in the ordinary course of business, and which might affect the insurer's decision on whether to accept the insurance and whether to increase the premium. "Known to the insured" means actual knowledge; "ought to be known by the insured in the ordinary course of business" includes not only the circumstances that the insurer has already inquired about, but also other circumstances that the insured ought to ascertain and control in the ordinary course of business. "Truthfully inform" means complete and correct disclosure; failure to disclose or incorrect disclosure of all or part of any material circumstance constitutes a failure to fulfill the duty of utmost good faith. The period during which the insured fulfills the duty of truthful disclosure shall commence from the time of making the insurance application, continue throughout the negotiation process between the parties, and last until the insurance contract is concluded. The insured is obliged to inform the insurer of any material circumstances that come to the insured's knowledge during the negotiation period, as well as circumstances that change from immaterial to material. The insured cargo vessel set sail on September 12, 1999, was reportedly abandoned by the crew on October 11 of the same year due to significant water ingress, and sank on October 14 in a severe storm 750 nautical miles from Durban, South Africa. As the buyer of the cargo, the Plaintiff, Jiangsu Overseas Enterprise Company, one month after the vessel set sail, failed to make necessary inquiries through various effective means regarding the current status of the cargo, and instead insured cargo that was already facing a marine casualty. This constitutes a breach of the duty of a bona fide insured to exercise due diligence in making reasonable inquiries and to truthfully disclose information. Existing evidence proves that at 20:38 on October 14, 1999, Jiangsu Overseas Enterprise Company received a fax from Company S about the cargo damage. At this time, although Jiangsu Overseas Enterprise Company had already applied for insurance with the Defendant, Shanghai Fengtai Insurance Company, the insurance contract had not yet been concluded. As the insured, Jiangsu Overseas Enterprise Company did not abide by the principle of utmost good faith by failing to inform the insurer of this material circumstance, known to it before the conclusion of the insurance contract, which was sufficient to affect the formation of the insurance contract. Jiangsu Overseas Enterprise Company's defense that it was unaware of the cargo damage at the time of insurance and therefore had no duty to disclose this circumstance is untenable. By reference to the UK case law that "if the insured conceals the fact that his vessel had already grounded and developed a leak before the contract was made, the insurance contract is void. The insured's failure to proactively disclose such a situation constitutes concealment of a material fact," the circumstances of this case are very similar to that precedent. Jiangsu Overseas Enterprise Company violated Article 17 of the UK Marine Insurance Act 1906, and Shanghai Fengtai Insurance Company has the right to declare the insurance contract void.

Furthermore, the risk of deck cargo is significantly higher than that of under-deck cargo, directly affecting the insurer's decision on whether to accept the insurance and the determination of the premium rate. The Plaintiff, Jiangsu Overseas Enterprise Company, received a copy of the shipping order as early as September 24, 1999, and was already aware that part of the cargo was stowed on deck. As the insured, Jiangsu Overseas Enterprise Company, at the time of insurance and thereafter, failed to disclose this material fact, which was sufficient to affect the formation of the insurance contract and the rights and obligations of both parties, to the insurer. This clearly constitutes a failure to fulfill the duty of truthful disclosure. Jiangsu Overseas Enterprise Company's defense that the stowage of timber on deck is a shipping custom that the insurer ought to know, and therefore it had no duty to disclose this circumstance, is untenable.

In summary, the Plaintiff, Jiangsu Overseas Enterprise Company, failed to conclude the insurance contract based on the principle of utmost good faith. The Defendant, Shanghai Fengtai Insurance Company, has the right to declare the insurance contract void and is not liable for insurance indemnity. Accordingly, the Shanghai Maritime Court rendered the following judgment on April 21, 2003:

The claims of the Plaintiff, Jiangsu Overseas Enterprise Group Co., Ltd., are not supported.

After the judgment was rendered, neither party appealed, and the judgment of first instance has become legally effective.
